definition: Animation execution quality (smoothness, polish, clean lines, visual appeal - HOW a motion moves) and choreographic intent (tactics, emotion, story, character purpose - WHY a sequence of actions was chosen) are separable axes that do not predict each other: a fight scene can have strong execution and weak intent (flashy but meaningless), weak execution and strong intent (technically rough but tactically and emotionally legible), or both - and across many real shipped examples, strong intent with weak execution reads as successful far more often than strong execution with weak intent does.
purpose: Give 'is this good animation' a second, independent question to check - not just how smoothly something moves, but whether the sequence of actions has a legible reason to exist - and name which of the two matters more when they conflict.
visible_effect: A sequence with strong intent but rough execution still reads as coherent and purposeful (readable tactics, escalating stakes, character-specific motivation for each beat) despite technical roughness (fewer frames, simpler lines, static camera); a sequence with strong execution but weak intent reads as visually impressive but forgettable, with no answer to 'why did the character just do that'.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: A viewer can consciously register execution quality (it 'looks smooth' or 'looks choppy') without consciously registering intent at all - the source's own diagnostic question is to deliberately check for it: 'read the intent behind it and not just the pixels. If you can follow and see the goal behind every movement, then chances are choreography is winning.'
physical_interpretation: None - a narrative/design-intent distinction, not a physical one.
use_cases: evaluating or critiquing a finished action sequence on two independent axes rather than one blended impression

deciding where to spend limited production budget when both cannot be fully afforded at once - the source's own repeated real examples (Naruto vs. Pain, One Punch Man S2's Garou alley fight, Dragon Ball Super's Goku vs. Beerus, 2016 Berserk) all spend the budget on intent (tactics, spacing, weight) over polish (clean lines, camera movement, frame count) and are judged to still succeed
non_use_cases: a purely technical/demo context with no story or character stakes at all, where there is no 'intent' axis to separate from execution in the first place
treating the two as always tradeable one-for-one - the source's own best examples (a cited Demon Slayer sequence) have both at once, which it calls out as the actual ideal rather than a forced choice
interactions: appeal (compiled principle) - a related but narrower, POSE-level judgement (does this one pose express this character); this entry is about a whole SEQUENCE's purpose across multiple actions, a different scope than one pose's appeal

ai/review.js QUALITY_LAYERS - this entry's 'intent' axis is a striking, independently-arrived-at real-world match for that module's own Layer 1, 'intent and purpose' ('measured: partly, by: the AcceptanceSpec, when one is supplied - otherwise nothing here knows what the shot is FOR'), and its 'execution' axis matches Layers 4 onward (timing, spacing, weight and mechanics, contacts, arcs, overlap, VFX, micro-polish) - the same top-vs-rest split this source arrives at from anime criticism, Cadence's own quality hierarchy already arrived at from the directive

ai/review.js's own hierarchy-ordering principle ('layer beats severity... a blocking micro-polish defect is still less important than a higher layer problem') and its named anti-patterns ('do not add beautiful secondary motion to a weak pose') are the SAME asymmetry this entry's real examples independently demonstrate: intent/purpose problems matter more than execution/polish ones, not the reverse

style_variations.anime: the source's own native domain, with real shipped examples on both sides of the split
style_variations.game_combat: the equivalent split already exists in this corpus's own game-design sources - Sakurai's four-phase model (this batch, video 39) is squarely about EXECUTION (timing, sharpness at contact), while this entry's 'intent' axis is closer to why a designer chose a given move's tactical role at all

cadence_representation: A precise match for an already-declared, already-ordered gap: `ai/review.js QUALITY_LAYERS` already puts 'intent and purpose' at layer 1 - the TOP of Part 14's thirteen-layer hierarchy - and already states plainly that nothing in this build knows what a shot is FOR unless a caller supplies an `AcceptanceSpec`. This entry is real-world, cross-domain evidence that ranking intent above execution (the hierarchy's own ordering) is the right call, not an arbitrary directive choice - multiple real, shipped, technically-rough sequences are judged successful specifically because their INTENT still reads, exactly the case Cadence's own hierarchy is built to prioritize once an AcceptanceSpec exists to check against.
control_surface: `AcceptanceSpec` (when supplied) is the only existing surface that lets `ai/review.js` say anything about layer 1 at all; without one, intent is entirely unmeasured, which this build already states honestly rather than defaulting to 'passing'.
detection_and_measurement_methods: Layers 4 and below (timing, spacing, weight/mechanics proxies, contacts, arcs, chain propagation, micro-polish) are measured or partly measured today via `ai/motion.js` and related modules - the EXECUTION axis this entry names. The INTENT axis (does this sequence of actions serve a legible tactical/emotional/narrative purpose) has no measurement path in this build at all beyond checking a supplied `AcceptanceSpec`'s own stated goal against a result - the same honestly-stated gap `QUALITY_LAYERS` already reports for layer 1.
generation_or_modification_methods: None - authoring INTENT (choosing why a character performs a given move, in what narrative or tactical order) is a human authorial decision entirely upstream of any tool in `ai/plan.js`, which only executes already-decided actions.
failure_modes: judging a sequence's quality purely by execution polish (smoothness, frame count, camera work) while missing whether the underlying sequence of actions has any legible purpose - the source's own repeated warning

over-investing production budget in execution polish at the expense of intent when the two compete for the same limited resources, when the source's own examples suggest the opposite trade consistently reads better
the two named anti-patterns `ai/review.js` already states for the SAME underlying asymmetry: polishing a lower layer while a higher one (including layer 1) is failing
roblox_considerations: None beyond the general point that a Roblox combat/ability system's animation budget faces the same real trade-off between execution polish and legible tactical intent, independent of the target engine.
examples: "read the intent behind it and not just the pixels. If you can follow and see the goal behind every movement, then chances are choreography is winning. And if it's much simpler but beautiful with unimpactful movement, then animation is winning" (video @ 06:40-06:52)

One Punch Man season 2's Garou alley fight, cited as weak execution ('the frames got chunky') but strong intent: 'the camera barely moves, the lighting's low, yet every dodge, sweep, encounter tells you exactly who's controlling the tempo. That's choreography carrying bad animation' (video @ 05:42-06:00)

2016 Berserk, cited the same way: 'ugly frames, but the choreography respects the characters fighting... the sword arcs are deliberately huge so you can feel the weight, the camera cuts wide so you can read the spacing' (video @ 06:20-06:34)

the explicit warning for the opposite failure: "if this scene was all flash and no meaning, just [the character] doing flips for no reason and swinging his sword senselessly, it wouldn't have hit the same" (video @ 02:27-02:33)
